produced_by: claude-fable-5-1, ten parallel labellers over a stratified sample; spot-checked by claude-opus-5 on low-confidence labels and on disagreements with the classifier
notes: 374 reviews: 20 per predicted category plus a random tail, so per-category figures are possible without the sample being purely the classifier's own view.

The two subsets now have different jobs and must not be merged. The 314 stratified labels are TRAINING DATA: `census fit` builds the category anchors from them. Any figure measured over them says what the anchors memorised. The 60 random labels are held back from fitting entirely and are the only ones that measure anything, which is also why `census evaluate` reports the subsets separately rather than blending them.

Measured on the held-out random subset, primary agreement went from 51.1% to 72.3% on the clear-cut reviews when the anchors were fitted rather than written (12 reviews gained, 2 lost; McNemar exact p=0.013). Mention macro F1 over the whole set went 0.300 to 0.557. The gain is concentrated in `verdict`, which written descriptions could barely find at all: 5 of 17 held-out verdict reviews before, 11 of 17 after.

Fitting costs the rarest categories. `controls`, `community`, `performance` and `multiplayer` have too few labels to learn from and now lose every contest to categories that were fitted, so the classifier stops predicting them: `audio` mention F1 fell 0.21 to 0.10 and `compatibility` 0.46 to 0.22. Scoring each category against its own corpus average was tried as a fix, rescued the tail exactly as intended, and was rejected because it destroyed the common categories badly enough to lose on macro F1 as well (0.328 against 0.557). The real fix is labels for those categories, not a scoring trick.

Because no person has checked these labels, results measured against this set are AGREEMENT WITH A MODEL and must never be reported as accuracy. Two language models agreeing can be wrong together, and the sarcasm and category-boundary cases where this classifier is weakest are exactly where that correlation is strongest.

Spot check found the reference labels better than the classifier on roughly nine of ten disagreements: 'good' was classified as price, 'amauzing' as audio, and a Chinese review about exploration and skills as bugs. One review of 374 received seven secondary categories, which edges towards over-assignment on long text.
Set human_verified to true only once a person has labelled a subset independently, and record how large that subset was.

90 of the 374 labels (24.1%) are flagged ambiguous because the labeller said the call was genuinely contested. Contested reviews stay far harder for the classifier whichever anchors it uses: on the held-out random subset it agreed with 23.1% of them before fitting and 30.8% after, against 51.1% and 72.3% for the clear-cut ones. Reference ambiguity therefore explains part of the disagreement and never all of it.

Known inconsistency: the labelling instructions did not say what to do with a bare verdict plus one thin specific ('super fun, worth every penny'). Labellers resolved it both ways, sometimes in near-identical cases, so verdict-versus-specific boundaries in this set are not internally consistent. Fix the rule before producing the next set.

Recurring contested boundaries, all worth addressing in the taxonomy rather than the classifier: in-game anecdotes and character jokes sitting between story and gameplay; 'replayability' sitting between content and gameplay; genre comparisons ('X-Com meets FTL') naming no mechanic; and balance complaints sitting between gameplay and difficulty.

Taxonomy gaps found by labellers: sequel and port requests ('We need RE2', 'Need this on the Switch!'), animation speed, and content-free dismissals such as 'I find this game childish' have no category and were forced into verdict.
